p.src: Overview: Two constrained systems show why Lagrangian mechanics is so effective: once suitable coordinates have been chosen, the equations of motion and their conservation laws follow without an explicit calculation of the constraint forces. The same examples then lead to Hamiltonian mechanics, in which coordinates and momenta form phase space, the harmonic oscillator becomes a rigid rotation, and Hamilton’s two first-order equations replace each second-order Euler–Lagrange equation.

en: Overview: Two constrained systems show why Lagrangian mechanics is so effective: once suitable coordinates have been chosen, the equations of motion and their conservation laws follow without an explicit calculation of the constraint forces. The same examples then lead to Hamiltonian mechanics, in which coordinates and momenta form phase space, the harmonic oscillator becomes a rigid rotation, and Hamilton’s two first-order equations replace each second-order Euler–Lagrange equation.
ja: 概観: 二つの拘束系は、ラグランジュ力学がなぜこれほど有効であるかを示している。適切な座標を選んでしまえば、運動方程式とその保存則は、拘束力を陽に計算することなく導かれる。同じ例はさらにハミルトン力学へと導く。そこでは座標と運動量が位相空間をなし、調和振動子は剛体回転となり、ハミルトンの二つの一階方程式が各々の二階のオイラー–ラグランジュ方程式に取って代わる。
zh: 概述: 两个约束系统说明了为什么拉格朗日力学如此有效：一旦选定了合适的坐标，运动方程及其守恒定律便随之得出，而无需显式计算约束力。随后，同样的例子又引向哈密顿力学：在其中坐标与动量构成相空间，谐振子化为刚性旋转，而哈密顿的两个一阶方程取代了每一个二阶的欧拉–拉格朗日方程。

p.src:
The wedge has kinetic energy $T_{M}=\frac{M}{2}\dot X^2.$ The particle’s horizontal velocity is $\dot X+\dot x$, while its vertical velocity is $\dot x$. Its kinetic energy is consequently $T_m=\frac{m}{2}\left[(\dot X+\dot x)^2+\dot x^2\right].$ Taking the zero of gravitational potential at $x=0$, we have $V=mgx$. Thus $L=\frac{M}{2}\dot X^2
    +\frac{m}{2}\left[(\dot X+\dot x)^2+\dot x^2\right]
    -mgx.$

p.src: Instead of $q_i$ and $\dot q_i$, use $q_i$ and their conjugate momenta $p_i$. A state of a system with $n$ degrees of freedom requires $2n$ numbers in either description: positions and velocities, or positions and momenta. The bridge between them is $p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}.$ When these relations can be inverted for the velocities $\dot q_i(q,p)$, define $H(q,p)=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L(q,\dot q).$ The velocities on the right are then eliminated in favor of $q$ and $p$. This invertibility is the regular Legendre-transform assumption. Singular Lagrangians require the more general theory of constraints; they are not handled by this elementary construction.

  \end{aligned}$

  &=\sum_i\left(\dot q_i\,\delta p_i
       +p_i\,\delta\dot q_i
       -\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}\delta q_i
       -\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}\delta\dot q_i\right).
  \end{aligned}$ 由于$\partial L/\partial\dot q_i=p_i$，两个$\delta\dot q_i$项相消。欧拉–拉格朗日方程给出$\partial L/\partial q_i=\dot p_i$，于是剩下 $\delta H=\sum_i\left(\dot q_i\,\delta p_i

An objection about units explains why the oscillator was written in the unfamiliar form of Eq. [eq:l6-rescaled-lagrangian]. Begin instead with the ordinary coordinate $x$: $L=\frac{m}{2}\dot x^2-\frac{k}{2}x^2,
  \qquad
  \omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}.$ Choose $q=(km)^{1/4}x.$ Then $q^2=\sqrt{km}\,x^2$ and $\dot q^2=\sqrt{km}\,\dot x^2$, which converts Eq. [eq:l6-ordinary-oscillator] precisely into Eq. [eq:l6-rescaled-lagrangian]. The new $q$ is an adapted generalized coordinate, not a length, and its conjugate $p$ is not the ordinary mechanical momentum $p_x=m\dot x$.
